tried out from the blubber of a whale; especially, ordinary oil from the right whale, as distinguished from ''sperm-oil.''

{{smaller block|Make in a readiness all such caske as shalbe needfull for ''traine oyle,'' tallowe, or any thing else.

¶
'''train-road''' (trān′rōd), ''n.'' 1. On railroads, a temporary construction-track for transportation of materials, etc.—2. In ''mining'', a temporary track in a mine, used for light loads.

'''train-rope''' (trān′rōp), ''n.'' Same as ''train-tackle.''

'''train-tackle''' (trān′tak″l), ''n.'' See ''tackle.''

'''trainway''' (trān′wā), ''n.'' A platform hinged to a wharf, and forming a bridge from the wharf to the deck of a ferry-boat. ''E. H. Knight.''

'''trainy†''' (trā′ni), ''a.'' [< ''train''<sup>2</sup> + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] Greasy like train-oil.

{{smaller block|Where huge hogsheads sweat with ''trainy'' oil.
{{right|''Gay'', Trivia, ii. 252.}}}}

'''traipse''', ''v.'' and ''n.'' See ''trapes.''

'''traist†''', ''n.'' Same as ''trace''<sup>2</sup>. ''Chaucer.''

'''traise<sup>1</sup>†''', ''v. t.'' [ME. ''traisen'', ''traysen'', ''traissen'', ''trasshen'', < OF. ''traiss-'', stem of certain parts of ''trair'', betray: see ''tray''<sup>3</sup>.] To betray.

{{smaller block|This lechecraft, or heled thus to be,
Were wel sittynge, if that I were a fend,
To ''traysen'' a wight that trewe is unto me.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iv. 438.}}}}

{{smaller block|She hath the ''trasshed'' withoute wene.
{{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 3231.}}}}

'''traise<sup>2</sup>†''', ''v. i.'' A Middle English form of ''trace''<sup>1</sup>.

'''traison†''', '''traisoun†''', ''n.'' Middle English forms

¶
{{smaller block|Nor is the postposition of the nominative case to the verb against the use of the tongue; nor the ''trajection'' here so great but the Latine will admit the same order of the words.
{{right|''J. Mede'', Works (1672), iii. 1.}}}}

'''trajectory''' (trā-jek′tō-ri), ''n.''; pl. ''trajectories'' (-riz). [= F. ''trajectoire'', trajectory, OF. the end of a funnel, also adj., passing over, < ML. *''trajectorius'', neut. ''trajectorium'', a funnel, < L. ''trajicere'', pp. ''trajectus'', throw over: see ''traject.''] 1. The path described by a body moving under the action of given forces; specifically, the curve described by a projectile in its flight through the air. Compare ''range'', 4.—2. In ''geom.'', a curve which cuts all the curves or surfaces of a given system at a constant angle. When the constant angle is a right angle, the trajectory is called an ''orthogonal trajectory''.

'''trajetour†''', ''n.'' Same as ''tregetour''. ''Gower.''

'''trajetry†''', ''n.'' Same as ''tregetry''.

'''tralation†''' (trā-lā′shon), ''n.'' [= It. ''tralazione'', < L. ''tralatio''(''n''-), equiv. to ''translatio''(''n''-), a transferring, translation: see ''translation.''] A change in the use of a word, or the use of a word in a less proper but more significant sense.

{{smaller block|According to the broad ''tralation'' of his rude Rhemists.
{{right|''Bp. Hall'', Honour of Married Clergy, i. § 14.}}}}

It is to be paralleled with the Laocoön group of the Rhodian school.}}

'''traluce†''' (trā-lūs′), ''v. i.'' [= It. ''tralucere'', < L. ''tralucere'', ''translucere'', shine through: see ''translucent''.] To shine through. ''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas's Weeks, i. 2.

[< ''train''2 + ''-y''1.] Greasy like train-oil. {{smaller block|Where huge hogsheads sweat with ''trainy'' oil. {{right|''Gay'', Trivia, ii. 252.}}}} '''traipse''', ''v.'' and ''n.'' See ''trapes.'' '''traist†''', ''n.'' Same as ''trace''2. ''Chaucer.'' '''traise1†''', ''v. t.'' [ME. ''traisen'', ''traysen'', ''traissen'', ''trasshen'', < OF. ''traiss-'', stem of certain parts of ''trair'', betray: see ''tray''3.] To betray. {{smaller block|This lechecraft, or heled thus to be, Were wel sittynge, if that I were a fend, To ''traysen'' a wight that trewe is unto me. {{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iv. 438.}}}} {{smaller block|She hath the ''trasshed'' withoute wene. {{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 3231.}}}} '''traise2†''', ''v. i.'' A Middle English form of ''trace''1. '''traison†''', '''traisoun†''', ''n.'' Middle English forms of ''treason.'' '''trait''' (trāt, in Great Britain trā), ''n.'' [< OF. ''trait'', ''traict'', a line, stroke, feature, tract, etc., F. ''trait'', a line, stroke, point, feature, fact, act, etc., = Pr. ''trait'', ''trag'', ''trah'' = It. ''tratto'', a line, etc., < L. ''tractus'', a drawing, course: see ''tract''1, ''n.'', of which ''trait'' is a doublet. Cf. also ''trace''2, orig. ''trais'', pl. of OF. ''trait''.] 1. A stroke; a touch. {{smaller block|By this single ''trait'', Homer makes an essential difference between the Iliad and Odyssey. {{right|''W. Broome'', Notes on the Odyssey, i. 9.}} From talk of war to ''traits'' of pleasantry. {{right|''Tennyson'', Lancelot and Elaine.}}}} 2. A distinguishing or peculiar feature; a peculiarity: as, a ''trait'' of character. {{smaller block|He had all the Puritanic ''traits'', both good and evil. {{right|''Hawthorne'', Scarlet Letter, Int., p. 8.}} One of the most remarkable ''traits'' in modern Egyptian superstition is the belief in written charms. {{right|''E. W. Lane'', Modern Egyptians, I. 318.}}}} '''traiterie†''', ''n.'' An old spelling of ''traitory''. '''traitor''' (trā′tọr), ''n.'' and ''a.'' [Early mod. E. also ''traitour''; < ME. ''traitour'', ''traytour'', ''treitur'', < OF. ''traitor'', ''traitur'', ''traiteur'', ''traistre'', F. ''traître'' = Pr. ''trahire'', ''traire'', ''trahidor'', ''traidor'', ''traitor'' = Sp. Pg. ''traidor'' = It. ''traditore'', < L. ''traditor'', one who betrays, a betrayer, traitor, lit. ‘one who delivers,’ and hence in LL. also a teacher, < ''tradere'', give up, deliver: see ''tradition'', ''tray''3, and cf. ''traditor''.] '''I.''' ''n.'' 1. One who violates his allegiance and betrays his country; one who is guilty of treason. See ''treason''. {{smaller block|God wole not that it be longe in the Hondes of ''Traytoures'' ne of Synneres, be thei Cristene or othere. {{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 74.}}}} {{smaller block|Alle tho that ne wolde not come, he lete hem well wite that thei sholde haue as streyte Iustice as longed to theuis and ''traytoures''. {{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), ii. 205.}}}} {{smaller block|William's Fortune secures him as well at home against ''Traitors'' as in the Field against his Enemies. {{right|''Baker'', Chronicles, p. 25.}}}} {{smaller block|There is no difference, in point of morality, whether a man calls me ''traitor'' in one word, or says I am one hired to betray my religion and sell my country. {{right|''Swift.''}}}} '''2.''' One who betrays any trust; a person guilty of perfidy or treachery; one who violates confidence reposed in him. {{smaller block|If you flatter him, you are a great ''traitor'' to him. {{right|''Bacon.''}}}} ='''Syn.''' 1. ''Rebel'', etc. See ''insurgent''. '''II.''' ''a.'' Of or pertaining to a traitor; traitorous. {{smaller block|And there is now this day no gretter treson thanne a gentille woman to yeue her selff to a ''traitour'' fals churle, blamed with vices, for there is mani of hem deceiued bi the foule and grete fals othes that the fals men vsen to swere to the women. {{right|''Knight of La Tour Landry'', p. 2.}}}} {{smaller block|Their silent war of lilies and of roses, Which Tarquin view'd in her fair face's field, In their pure ranks his ''traitor'' eye encloses. {{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 73.}}}} '''traitor†''' (trā′tọr), ''v. t.'' [< ''traitor'', ''n.''] To act the traitor toward; betray. {{smaller block|But time, it ''traitors'' me. {{right|''Lithgow.'' (''Imp. Dict.'')}}}} '''traitoress''' (trā′tọr-es), ''n.'' [< ''traitor'' + ''-ess.''] A female traitor; a traitress. {{smaller block|Fortune, . . . The false ''trayteresse'' pervers. {{right|''Chaucer'', Death of Blanche, l. 813.}}}} '''traitorful†''' (trā′tọr-fu̇l), ''a.'' [ME. ''traitourfull''; < ''traitor'' + ''-ful.''] Traitorous; treacherous. {{smaller block|My ''traitourfull'' torne [action] he turment my tene. {{right|''York Plays'', p. 316.}}}} '''traitorism''' (trā′tọr-izm), ''n.'' [< ''traitor'' + ''-ism.''] A betrayal. [Rare.] {{smaller block|The loyal clergy . . . are charged with ''traitorism'' of their principles. ''Roger North'', Examen, p. 323. (''Davies.'')}} '''traitorly†''' (trā′tọr-li), ''a.'' [< ''traitor'' + ''-ly''1.] Treacherous; perfidious. {{smaller block|These ''traitorly'' rascals, whose miseries are to be smiled at, their offences being so capital. ''Shak.'', W. T., iv. 4. 821.}} '''traitorous''' (trā′tọr-us), ''a.'' [Formerly also ''traiterous''; < ME. ''traitorous''; < ''traitor'' + ''-ous.''] 1. Guilty of treason; in general, treacherous; perfidious; faithless. {{smaller block|More of his [majesty's] friends have lost their lives in this rebellion than of his ''traitorous'' subjects. {{right|''Addison'', Freeholder, No. 31.}}}} 2. Consisting in treason; characterized by treason; implying breach of allegiance; perfidious: as, a ''traitorous'' scheme or conspiracy. {{smaller block|''Vol.'' My name 's Volturtius, I know Pomtinius. ''Pom.'' But he knows not you, While you stand out upon these ''traitorous'' terms. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Catiline, iv. 7.}}}} '''traitorously''' (trā′tọr-us-li), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''traiterously, treterously''; < ''traitorous'' + ''-ly''2.] In a traitorous manner; in violation of allegiance and trust; treacherously; perfidiously. {{smaller block|They had ''traitorously'' endeavoured to subvert the fundamental laws. {{right|''Clarendon.''}}}} '''traitorousness''' (trā′tọr-us-nes), ''n.'' The quality of being traitorous or treacherous; treachery. ''Bailey'', 1727. '''traitory†''' (trā′tọr-i), ''n.'' [ME. ''traitorie'', ''traiterye'', < OF. *''traitorie'', < ''traitor'', a traitor: see ''traitor''.] Treachery; betrayal; treason. {{smaller block|Tho com another companye
That had ydon the ''traiterye'',
The harm, the grete wikkednesse,
That any herte couthe gesse. {{right|''Chaucer'', House of Fame, l. 1812.}}}} '''traitress''' (trā′tres), ''n.'' [< F. ''traîtresse''; as ''traitor'' + ''-ess''.] A woman who betrays her trust; a perfidious woman; a female traitor: often used in a weakened, half-playful sense. {{smaller block|Ah, little ''traitress!'' none must know . . .
What vanity full dearly bought,
Joined to thine eye's dark witchcraft, drew
My spell-bound steps to Benvenue. {{right|''Scott'', L. of the L., vi. 28.}}}} '''traject''' (trā-jekt′), ''v. t.'' [< L. ''trajectus'', pp. of ''trajicere'' (LL. also rarely ''transjacere''), throw or cast over, carry over, ship over, transport, also transfix, < ''trans'', through, across, + ''jacere'', throw: see ''jet''1.] To throw or cast (across or through). [Rare.] {{smaller block|Thou knowst that to be Cerberus, and him
The ferriman who from the rivers brim
''Trajected'' thee. {{right|''Heywood'', Dialogues (Works, ed. Pearson, 1874, VI. 236).}}}} {{smaller block|If the sun's light be ''trajected'' through three or more cross prisms successively. {{right|''Newton'', Opticks, I. i., Exper. 10.}}}} '''traject''' (traj′ekt), ''n.'' [< OF. ''traject, trajet,'' a ferry, a passage over, = It. ''tragetto, tragitto,'' < L. ''trajectus,'' a passage over, < ''trajicere,'' throw over: see ''traject, v.'' Cf. ''treget.''] 1†. A ferry; a passage or place for passing over water with boats (by some commentators said to mean the boat itself). {{smaller block|Bring them, I pray thee, with imagin'd speed
Vnto the ''tranect'' [read ''traiect,'' i. e. ''traject,'' as in various modern editions], to the common ferry
Which trades to Venice. {{right|''Shak.,'' M. of V., iii. 4. 54 (folio 1623).}}}} 2. A trajectory. [Rare.] {{smaller block|The ''traject'' of comets. {{right|''Is. Taylor.'' (''Imp. Dict.'')}}}} 3. The act of throwing across or transporting; transmission; transference. [Rare.] {{smaller block|At the best, however, this ''traject'' [that of printing from Asia] was but that of the germ of life, which Sir W. Thomson, in a famous discourse, suggested had been carried to this earth from some other sphere by meteoric agency. {{right|''Athenæum.'' (''Imp. Dict.'')}}}} '''trajection''' (trā-jek′shọn), ''n.'' [= It. ''trajezione,'' < L. ''trajectio(n-),'' a crossing over, passage, transposition (of words), < ''trajicere,'' throw over, convey over: see ''traject.''] 1. The act of trajecting; a casting or darting through or across; a crossing; a passage. {{smaller block|My due for thy ''trajection'' downe here lay. {{right|''Heywood,'' Dialogues (Works, ed. Pearson, 1874, VI. 232).}}}} {{smaller block|Of this sort might be the spectre at the Rubicon, Cæsar hesitating that ''trajection.'' {{right|''Evelyn,'' True Religion, I. 144.}}}} 2. In ''gram.'' and ''rhet.,'' transposition: same as ''hyperbaton'' (''a''). [Rare.] {{smaller block|Nor is the postposition of the nominative case to the verb against the use of the tongue; nor the ''trajection'' here so great but the Latine will admit the same order of the words. {{right|''J. Mede'', Works (1672), iii. 1.}}}} '''trajectory''' (trā-jek′tō-ri), ''n.''; pl. ''trajectories'' (-riz). [= F. ''trajectoire'', trajectory, OF. the end of a funnel, also adj., passing over, < ML. *''trajectorius'', neut. ''trajectorium'', a funnel, < L. ''trajicere'', pp. ''trajectus'', throw over: see ''traject.''] 1. The path described by a body moving under the action of given forces; specifically, the curve described by a projectile in its flight through the air. Compare ''range'', 4.—2. In ''geom.'', a curve which cuts all the curves or surfaces of a given system at a constant angle. When the constant angle is a right angle, the trajectory is called an ''orthogonal trajectory''. '''trajetour†''', ''n.'' Same as ''tregetour''. ''Gower.'' '''trajetry†''', ''n.'' Same as ''tregetry''. '''tralation†''' (trā-lā′shon), ''n.'' [= It. ''tralazione'', < L. ''tralatio''(''n''-), equiv. to ''translatio''(''n''-), a transferring, translation: see ''translation.''] A change in the use of a word, or the use of a word in a less proper but more significant sense. {{smaller block|According to the broad ''tralation'' of his rude Rhemists. {{right|''Bp. Hall'', Honour of Married Clergy, i. § 14.}}}} '''tralatition†''' (tral-ạ̄-tish′ọn), ''n.'' [Irreg. for ''tralation'' (after ''tralatitious'').] A departure from the literal use of words; a metaphor. '''tralatitious†''' (tral-ạ̄-tish′us), ''a.'' [=It. ''tralatizio'', < L. ''tralaticius'', ''tralatitius'', equiv. to ''translaticius'', ''translatitius'', < ''translatus'', pp. of ''transferre'', transfer: see ''translate''.] Metaphorical; not literal. {{smaller block|Unless we could contrive a perfect set of new words, there is no speaking of the Deity without using our old ones in a ''tralatitious'' sense. ''Stackhouse'', Hist. Bible, iv. 1.}} '''tralatitiously†''' (tral-ạ̄-tish′us-li), ''adv.'' Metaphorically; not in a literal sense. {{smaller block|Written Language is ''tralatitiously'' so called, because it is made to represent to the Eye the same Letters and Words which are pronounced. {{right|''Holder'', Elements of Speech, p. 8.}}}} '''tralineate†''' (trạ̄-lin′ẹ̄-āt), ''v. i.'' [After It. ''tralignare'', degenerate, < L. ''trans'', across, + ''linea'', line: see ''line''2.] To deviate in course or direction. {{smaller block|If you ''tralineate'' from your father's mind, What are you else but of a bastard-kind? {{right|''Dryden'', Wife of Bath, l. 396.}}}} '''Trallian''' (tral′ian), ''a.'' [< L. ''Trallianus'' (< Gr. Τραλλιανός), of Tralles, < ''Tralles'', also ''Trallis'', < Gr. Τράλλεις, also Τράλλις, a city of Lydia.] Of or pertaining to the ancient Greek city of Tralles, in Asia Minor, or its inhabitants.—{{smaller|'''Trallian school''', a school of Greek Hellenistic sculpture of the third century {{sc|b. c.}}, of which the great surviving work is the large group known as the Farnese Bull, in the Museum at Naples. This important work, while transgressing the proper limitations of sculpture in the round, exhibits originality, vigor, skill in composition, and a high decorative quality. It is to be paralleled with the Laocoön group of the Rhodian school.}} [[File:century v08 p0227 c3f1.png|center|312px]] {{c|Trallian School of Sculpture.—The group called the Farnese Bull, in the Museo Nazionale, Naples.}} '''traluce†''' (trā-lūs′), ''v. i.'' [= It. ''tralucere'', < L. ''tralucere'', ''translucere'', shine through: see ''translucent''.] To shine through. ''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas's Weeks, i. 2.
